meta.title: File Storage and Sync
meta.summary: Store files in the cloud and keep them in sync across a person's devices, like Dropbox or Google Drive.

functional: Upload, download and delete files and folders
Sync changes to every device signed in to the account
Keep earlier versions of a file
Handle edits made offline on two devices
nonFunctional: Never lose a committed file (11 nines durability)
Changes reach other online devices within 5 seconds
Upload only what changed, not the whole file

scale.label: Storage
scale.value: ~500 PB of blocks before deduplication (assuming an average file of about 5 MB)

nodes.label: Laptop
nodes.description: Desktop app watching a synced folder

nodes.label: Phone
nodes.description: Another device on the same account

nodes.label: WAF
nodes.description: Inspects every API and notifier request before the load balancer: managed rule sets, per-IP and per-account rate rules, bot control

nodes.label: Change Notifier
nodes.description: Holds a long-poll from every online device and answers it when the account's sequence passes the device's cursor, or with "nothing new" after about 50 s so the load balancer's 60 s idle timeout never cuts it

nodes.label: Metadata API
nodes.description: Files, versions, block lists, the account journal and sharing; signs upload and download URLs. Autoscaled: about 70 tasks at the ~140,000 requests/s peak (2,000 per task)

nodes.label: Block Storage
nodes.description: 4 MB blocks named by their SHA-256 hash, written once (create-only) and never overwritten, so identical blocks are stored once

nodes.label: Metadata DB
nodes.description: Sharded by account, so one account's changes are ordered on one shard. Holds files, versions, each account's journal (the sync cursor) and the per-account block index. One writer cannot take 50,000 multi-statement commits/s, so it is many shards, each primary-standby across zones

nodes.label: Change Log
nodes.description: Wake-up events partitioned by account id; the journal in the Metadata DB stays the source of truth

flows.title: Upload a changed file
flows.summary: Only the blocks that changed travel; the commit is a small metadata write.

steps.label: split into 4 MB blocks, hash each
steps.detail: The client cuts the file into fixed-size blocks and hashes each one. An in-place edit changes one or two blocks, so only those travel. An insertion near the start shifts every later block boundary, so fixed blocks all change; systems that care cut blocks at content-defined boundaries (a rolling hash) instead, at the cost of variable block sizes.

steps.label: POST /commit (block hashes)
steps.detail: The client first proposes the new version as a list of block hashes, without sending any file data. A trace id starts here and is passed on every hop, so one commit can be followed through the API, the database and the notifier.

steps.label: inspect, then forward
steps.detail: Managed rule sets, per-IP and per-account rate rules and bot control run before anything reaches the services, so a client stuck in a retry loop is throttled here.

steps.label: which hashes does this account have?
steps.detail: The account's block index says which of these hashes it already references, from earlier versions or other files. Blocks that only other users hold are not skipped: trusting a hash alone would let anyone who learns a hash claim, then download, someone else's file. Those still upload, and storage keeps one copy because the name is the hash.
steps.payload:
SELECT hash FROM account_blocks
WHERE account_id = 9 AND hash IN ('a41f…','9be0…','c9e1…')

steps.label: upload c9e1 to signed URL
steps.detail: The API signs a short-lived, create-only URL for each missing block that pins the block's SHA-256, so storage rejects bytes that do not match the name. Bytes never pass through the API servers.

steps.label: PUT block c9e1
steps.detail: The client uploads straight to object storage. A large upload is many independent blocks, so a dropped connection only retries one block. The checksum header must match the signed one and If-None-Match makes the write create-only, so no client can overwrite a block other files share.
steps.payload:
PUT https://blocks…/c9e1…?X-Amz-Signature=…
x-amz-checksum-sha256: <base64 of c9e1…>
If-None-Match: *
Content-Length: 4194304

steps.label: POST /commit (retry)
steps.detail: The same request again, now that every block is uploaded. It carries the client's commit id, so if this response is lost and the client retries once more, the API finds the version that id already created and returns it instead of a 409 against its own commit.

steps.label: HEAD c9e1
steps.detail: The client said it uploaded the block; the API checks before any version references it, so a buggy client cannot commit a file whose bytes are missing.

steps.label: move head 7 to 8 + journal, one transaction
steps.detail: The head moves only if the file is still at the version the client edited. The UPDATE takes the row lock, so two concurrent commits from v7 cannot both win, which a separate SELECT-then-INSERT check would allow. The same transaction records the new blocks in the account's index and appends to the account's journal with its next sequence number (1042): the cursor every device syncs from.

steps.label: account 9 at seq 1042
steps.detail: The commit is already durable in the journal; this event only wakes the notifiers. It is keyed by account id so one account's events stay in order. If the publish fails or the API dies first, nothing is lost: a relay in the API re-publishes journal rows the stream has not acknowledged, and devices catch up from their cursor anyway.

flows.title: Another device picks up the change
flows.summary: A waiting long-poll is answered, then the device fetches only the blocks it lacks.

steps.label: GET /changes?cursor=1041 (held open)
steps.detail: The phone keeps one request open and remembers a cursor: the last journal sequence it has applied. If the connection drops it reconnects with the same cursor and misses nothing.

steps.label: consume account events
steps.detail: Every notifier instance consumes the Change Log and keeps the latest sequence it has seen for each account whose requests it holds. It never reads one account's history from the log: that lives in the journal.

steps.label: GET /delta?cursor=1041
steps.detail: The notifier only said that something changed. The phone asks the Metadata API what changed since its cursor, so a lost notification or a reconnect never loses a change.

steps.label: journal after 1041 + block lists
steps.detail: One indexed range read on the account's shard returns every change since the cursor, in order.
steps.payload:
SELECT j.seq, v.file_id, v.version, v.blocks
FROM journal j JOIN versions v USING (file_id, version)
WHERE j.account_id = 9 AND j.seq > 1041
ORDER BY j.seq LIMIT 1000

steps.label: GET block c9e1
steps.detail: The phone already has two of the blocks from the previous version, so it downloads only the new one, and checks its SHA-256 against the name before using it.

steps.label: assemble v8, save cursor 1042
steps.detail: The file is rebuilt from blocks it had plus the new one and swapped into place atomically. Only then does the phone save cursor 1042, so a crash halfway simply repeats the delta.

flows.title: Conflicting offline edit
flows.summary: Two devices edited the same version; nothing is lost and the user decides.

steps.label: edited v7 while offline
steps.detail: The phone edited the file without a connection, starting from version 7. Meanwhile the laptop committed version 8.

steps.label: move head to 8 if still 7
steps.detail: The phone never saw version 8, so it proposes its edit as the next version after 7.
steps.payload: UPDATE files SET head = 8 WHERE id = 42 AND head = 7;  -- 0 rows

steps.label: rejected: head is already 8
steps.detail: The compare-and-set fails because the laptop's commit moved the file on. Silently overwriting would lose the laptop's work.

steps.label: save as conflicted copy
steps.detail: The client keeps both: version 8 under the original name and its own edit as a conflicted copy, which it uploads as a new file. Text editors could merge instead; a general file store cannot.

notes.text: Content-addressed blocks give deduplication for free: identical blocks across versions and users are stored once. The cost is reference counting or a garbage collector (a background job, not drawn here) before any block can be deleted; it only deletes blocks unreferenced for days, so it cannot race a commit that is about to reference one.
File bytes never pass through the API servers. Signed URLs send uploads and downloads straight to object storage, so the API only handles small metadata requests.

Shard metadata by account (or by shared folder) so one account's changes live on one shard and can be ordered by a single sequence. A shared folder with thousands of members, or one account with millions of files, makes its shard hot; such namespaces are moved to a shard of their own.
Notifications can be lost without losing changes: a device that missed one asks the Metadata API for everything after its saved cursor, read from the journal.

Each notifier instance must hear about every account whose long-polls it holds. Here every instance reads the whole Change Log, which works while events are small (50,000/s × ~200 bytes ≈ 10 MB/s), but every extra reader adds stream reads (Kinesis shares 2 MB/s per shard among readers unless enhanced fan-out is used). With many instances, assign log partitions to instances and route each device to the instance that owns its account, or put a pub/sub layer keyed by account in between.

Signed URLs expire in minutes, cover one block and pin its SHA-256, and the write is create-only, so a client cannot overwrite or poison a block other files share. (S3 checks a signed SHA-256 checksum header; where storage cannot check SHA-256, new blocks must be rehashed before a commit may reference them.) The skip-upload check only counts blocks the same account already references. Blocks are encrypted at rest and the bucket is never public.

The WAF covers the API and notifier hostnames: managed rule sets, per-IP and per-account rate rules and bot control, so credential stuffing and runaway clients stop at the edge. Block uploads and downloads go straight to object storage and bypass it; their protection is the short-lived, single-block signature.

slos.name: Sync API availability
slos.sli: Metadata requests answered without a 5xx, divided by all metadata requests, at the load balancer

slos.name: Changes reach other devices
slos.sli: Commits whose notification reaches waiting devices within the threshold, measured by the notifier from the commit time in the event to the long-poll answer

slos.name: Committed files stay complete
slos.sli: Committed versions whose blocks are all present in storage, checked by a daily audit sample. A sample cannot demonstrate 11 nines: the target is the storage design figure, and the audit exists to catch any loss event (a garbage collector or client bug), which pages at once.

alerts.when: Metadata API 5xx burning the error budget 14 times too fast over 1 hour and over 5 minutes (a slow burn, 6 times over 6 hours, opens a ticket instead)
alerts.why: Devices cannot commit or fetch changes right now.

alerts.when: Notifications later than 5 s burning the error budget 14 times too fast over 1 hour and over 5 minutes
alerts.why: Users see stale files on their other devices and start editing old versions, which creates conflicts.

alerts.when: The audit finds any committed version with a missing block
alerts.why: Data loss is the one failure users never forgive; stop garbage collection and investigate at once.

alerts.when: Change Log consumer lag above 30 s for 10 minutes
alerts.why: A cause, not yet a symptom: notifications will slow down if it keeps growing.

alerts.when: Oldest journal row not yet published to the Change Log above 30 s for 10 minutes
alerts.why: The relay is stuck: devices still converge from their cursors, but only when their long-poll times out, so propagation will slow down.

alerts.when: Any metadata shard above 70% CPU or commit p99 above 200 ms for 15 minutes
alerts.why: One huge shared folder or account can saturate its shard long before the fleet looks busy; move that namespace before its commits start failing.

alerts.when: Commit conflicts above 1% of commits for a day
alerts.why: Usually a client bug or slow notifications making devices edit stale versions.

signals.name: Blocks already stored on commit
signals.why: How much upload traffic deduplication saves; a sudden drop points at a client hashing bug.

signals.name: Open long-polls
signals.why: Should track online devices; a drop means devices are not reconnecting.

signals.name: Commit conflicts
signals.why: Every conflict is a user who has to sort out two copies.

signals.name: Journal entries per delta read
signals.why: Large deltas mean devices were offline or notifications are not arriving; a sudden rise across accounts points at the notifier.

debug.symptom: Changes take minutes to reach my other devices
steps: Check the propagation SLO: is it every account or a few?
Look at Change Log consumer lag; a backlog delays every notification.
Check open long-polls on the notifier: did devices drop their connections?
Follow one commit's trace from the API to the notifier answer.
Split by client version and region to rule out a bad release.
Check signed URL errors: expired or rejected signatures point at clock skew or key rotation.
Check object storage error rates and throttling.
Confirm the commit retry finds the uploaded blocks (dedup hit ratio).

debug.symptom: A user says one device shows an old version of a file
steps: Look up the file's head and the account's journal: did the commit happen at all?
Compare the device's last cursor (from its delta requests) with the journal head for the account.
If the cursor is behind, check whether the device holds a long-poll and whether the notifier saw the account's event.
If the device is up to date, look for a conflicted copy: the user may be looking at the losing edit.

questions.q: Why split files into blocks instead of uploading whole files?
questions.a: Only changed blocks travel, so a small edit to a large file uploads a few megabytes instead of the whole file. Content-addressed blocks are also stored once across versions and users. Uploads become many small retryable pieces, which handles flaky networks. Fixed-size blocks break on insertions, which shift every later boundary; content-defined chunking with a rolling hash fixes that.

questions.q: Two devices edit the same file offline. What happens when both come back online?
questions.a: The first commit wins because it matches the parent version; the second fails the compare-and-set. The second device keeps both versions by saving its edit as a conflicted copy, so nothing is lost. Automatic merging only works for formats the system understands, like text or documents.

questions.q: Millions of devices are online. How do they learn about changes without constant polling?
questions.a: Each device holds one long-poll or WebSocket open to the notifier, which answers it when the account's sequence passes the device's cursor. A device that reconnects asks the Metadata API for everything after its cursor, so a dropped notification is never a lost change. The notifier only says that something changed; the details come from the journal through the metadata API.

questions.q: A user deletes a file. When can its blocks be deleted from storage?
questions.a: Only when no version of any file references them, since blocks are shared across versions and users. Keep a reference count or run a mark-and-sweep garbage collector, and delay deletion by days so a bug or an undo cannot cause data loss. Old versions are kept for a retention period first.

questions.q: How would you shard the metadata database?
questions.a: By account or by shared folder namespace, so all changes for one namespace sit on one shard and can be ordered with a single sequence. Shared folders that span accounts are their own namespace. Very large namespaces may need splitting, which is the hard case.

questions.q: A user uploads a 50 GB video over a weak connection. How do you make that reliable?
questions.a: Each 4 MB block is uploaded independently with its own signed URL and retried on its own, so a dropped connection resumes from the last finished block. The commit happens only when all blocks are present, so a half-finished upload is never visible. Upload several blocks in parallel to use the bandwidth.
